title: Two conditions for any testimony to make the mind certain
source_text: XXI. Sed fatendum est istam Theologorum rationem sic nude propositam non omnem scrupulum ex animo tollere, nec per hoc inquirenti menti satisfieri. Ad hoc enim, ut testimonium & authoritas quaevis mentem nostram de re aliqua certam reddat, duo omnino requiruntur. Primo ut judicemus illum, qui testimonium perhibet, dignum esse cui fides adhibeatur, & fallere, vel non posse, vel non velle. Deinde ut certi simus tale testimonium vere ab eo perhiberi, nec esse fictitium & supposititium.
pass_a_gloss: But it must be confessed that this reason of the Theologians so nakedly proposed does not take every scruple from the mind, nor by this is the inquiring mind satisfied. For to this end, that any testimony and authority make our mind certain of some thing, two things are altogether required. First that we judge him who bears the testimony worthy to be believed, and that he either cannot or will not deceive. Second that we be certain such testimony is truly borne by him, and is not fictitious and supposed.
pass_b_english: Any testimony needs two: (1) witness worthy / cannot or will not deceive; (2) testimony truly his — not fictive/supposed.

lemmas.gloss: and is not fictitious and supposed

choices.why: Sets the dilemma leading to XXIII’s hard question.
rejected: divine authority alone, without knowing the word is God’s, settles the mind
